description: Split a 9x13 cake between two 9x5 loaf pans. Two loaves hold 16 cups against the 9x13's 14, so scale the batter by 1.14 and bake 10-15 minutes longer.

steps: Write down the recipe batter: 6 cups.
6 x 1.14 = 6.9 cups in total, about 3.4 cups per loaf pan.
The batter sits deeper than in the 9x13, so expect 10 to 15 minutes longer: 35 to 50 minutes.

faqs.answer: One 9x5 loaf pan holds 8 cups, and a scaled 9x13 recipe makes about 7 cups of batter, so it fits, but only just, and it bakes very deep and very long. Two pans are the better answer. If you only own one, bake the extra batter as muffins.
faqs.question: Can I use one loaf pan instead of two?

faqs.answer: Because the batter sits deeper. Heat has further to travel to reach the center of a loaf than the center of a sheet cake. King Arthur puts the difference at 10 to 15 minutes longer for a smaller, deeper pan, and that matches this swap.
faqs.question: Why is the bake longer?

faqs.answer: Yes for butter cakes, pound cakes, and one-bowl oil cakes, which all bake well deep. Sponge and angel food cakes do not suit deep pans, because they need a wide, shallow bake to hold their rise.
faqs.question: Can I bake a sheet cake recipe as a loaf at all?

faqs.answer: Half to two-thirds full, which is about 5.3 cups at most in a 9x5 loaf pan. Loaf batter climbs as it bakes, and an overfull loaf spills over the sides and burns onto the oven floor.
faqs.question: How full should each loaf be?

faqs.answer: Yes, if they sit on the same rack with air between them. Give each loaf an inch of space on all sides so the hot air can move. Rotate the pans front to back halfway through if your oven has a hot spot.
faqs.question: Do the two loaves bake evenly?

felicityNote: One loaf for the table, one for the freezer or a neighbour. That is the whole point of splitting a sheet cake into loaves.

formula.text: New batter = recipe batter x 1.14. Factor = new volume divided by old volume = 16 divided by 14 = 1.14.

howToSteps.name: Work out the factor
howToSteps.text: Two 9x5 loaf pans hold 16 cups and a 9x13 holds 14. Divide 16 by 14 and the factor is 1.14. This swap uses volume, because loaf pans are deeper than a sheet pan.

howToSteps.name: Scale every ingredient
howToSteps.text: Multiply each ingredient by 1.14, including the leavening. A recipe with 6 cups of batter becomes 6.9 cups in total.

howToSteps.name: Split the batter evenly
howToSteps.text: Divide the scaled batter between two greased 9x5 loaf pans, about half in each. Keep each loaf no more than two-thirds full, about 5.3 cups.

howToSteps.name: Bake longer, and test the center
howToSteps.text: Keep the oven temperature the recipe gives, but expect 10 to 15 minutes longer. Start checking at the recipe time and use a skewer in the center of each loaf.

lede: Two 9x5 loaf pans hold 16 cups between them and a 9x13 holds 14, so the loaves take about 14 percent more batter. Loaf pans are deeper than a sheet pan, so the bake runs 10 to 15 minutes longer.

title: 9x13 to Loaf Pans: Pan Converter
tutorial: Loaf pans are deep, and depth is why this swap runs on volume instead of area. A 9x13 pan is 2 inches deep and holds 14 cups. A 9x5 loaf pan is about 2.75 inches deep and holds 8 cups. Two of them hold 16 cups, so the volume factor is 16 divided by 14, which is 1.14. Area maths would give a different answer and the wrong one, because it ignores the extra depth.

A typical 9x13 cake makes about 6 cups of batter, which becomes 6.9 cups scaled, or about 3.4 cups in each loaf pan. That sits well under the two-thirds fill line for a 9x5 loaf, which is about 5.3 cups. The loaves have room to rise, and a loaf cake needs that room more than a sheet cake does, because the batter climbs a long way in a deep pan.

The bake runs longer, and that is the honest trade of this swap. Batter in a loaf pan sits deeper than batter in a sheet pan, so the heat takes longer to reach the center. King Arthur says a smaller, deeper pan can take 10 to 15 minutes longer, and that is the right expectation here. A 35-minute sheet cake becomes a 35 to 50 minute loaf bake. Start checking at the recipe time and trust the skewer, not the clock.

Watch the top. In a deep pan the top can set and brown before the center finishes, especially with a sugary batter. If the top darkens early, lay a sheet of foil loosely over the loaves and keep baking. The foil slows the browning without stopping the bake, and the center catches up.

Two loaves are the point of this swap, not a side effect. One loaf for the table and one for the freezer, or one for home and one for a neighbour. A sheet cake is hard to give away half of. A loaf is built for it. Wrap the second loaf once it is fully cool, and it freezes well for weeks.
